title: Utility-scale solar energy facilities – Effects on invertebrates in an arid environment
abstract: Attempts to reduce carbon emissions have seen a growth in renewable energy developments globally. “Green” alternatives also have impacts for biodiversity, but few studies assess the effects of solar energy facilities on invertebrate communities. We investigated effects of a concentrated solar power (CSP) trough facility on invertebrate communities in the arid Northern Cape province of South Africa. Epigaeic and flying invertebrates were sampled using pitfall and sticky traps in three habitats: solar field, power block and surrounding rangeland. There were no significant differences in abundance or order richness in either epigaeic or flying invertebrate communities across the three habitats. Shannon diversity was significantly lower in rangeland plots for epigaeic invertebrates, and significantly greater in solar field for flying invertebrates. Despite the lack of significant differences in order richness or abundance, community composition of both invertebrate groups differed significantly between habitats, but the two habitats within the plant only differed for epigaeic invertebrate assemblages. Differences in invertebrate densities and composition demonstrate an effect of construction of the facility on invertebrate communities. While facilities may have relatively small footprints, the rate at which the industry is expanding internationally suggests that further research on impacts and mitigation measures is needed.

## 1. Introduction

Efforts to reduce our reliance on fossil fuels by pursuing renewable energy alternatives can, paradoxically, have various harmful ecological impacts (Tsoutsos et al., 2005; Hernandez et al., 2014; Smith and Dwyer, 2016; Száz et al., 2016; Gasparatos et al., 2017). These impacts include habitat transformation and displacement (Smith and Dwyer, 2016; Gasparatos et al., 2017), bird collision with infrastructure (Loss et al., 2013; Smith and Dwyer, 2016; Visser et al., 2018), animaldrownings in evaporation ponds (Jeal et al., 2019), and the large volumes of water used in concentrated solar power (CSP) facilities introduce additional water stress in arid areas (Tsoutsos et al., 2005). Despite these negative effects, reducing carbon emissions to mitigate the effects of climate change on biodiversity is essential. Empirical research is urgently needed to understand the impacts of renewable energy facilities on biodiversity, to help inform siting of new generating facilities, management and mitigation efforts (Gibson et al., 2017).

The solar power industry is a fast-expanding provider of renewable

energy: global solar PV capacity grew by 50% in 2016 alone (https:// www.iea.org/publications/renewables2017/). Considering this rate of expansion, the paucity of empirical research assessing the environmental impact of Utility Scale Solar Energy (USSE) facilities is both surprising and concerning (Hernandez et al., 2014; Gibson et al., 2017; Guiller et al., 2017; Visser et al., 2018). Habitat loss is considered the most marked impact that USSE facilities have on biodiversity (Hernandez et al., 2014). Impacts vary with the taxa considered and the type of technology – 1) photovoltaic (PV) solar cells, 2) CSP towers and 3) CSP troughs (Kagan et al., 2014). Of the research done to date on the effects of USSE facilities on biodiversity, most has focused on birds, primarily on bird collisions with solar infrastructure and burning due to solar flux (limited to CSP facilities) (e.g. Kagan et al., 2014; Walston et al., 2016; Visser et al., 2018; Jeal et al., 2019). There is scant information about impacts on other fauna (Lovich and Ennen, 2011), particularly invertebrates (Guiller et al., 2017), even though invertebrates perform integral roles in ecosystem functioning (Weisser and Siemann, 2008).

PV solar panels reflect horizontally-polarized light that aquatic invertebrates use as visual cues to find water bodies (Horváth et al., 2010; Száz et al., 2016). Aquatic invertebrates can therefore mistake solar panels for water bodies, so the PV solar facilities are potential “ecological traps” that may encourage invertebrates to deposit their eggs on the panels, reducing reproductive success (Horváth et al., 2010). Ecological traps arise when novel environments are created that attract species to settle in low-quality habitats (Battin, 2004; Horváth et al., 2010). CSP trough facilities use parabolic mirror troughs as solar collectors, which could potentially also confuse invertebrates if the mirrors are perceived as a body of water. Increases in invertebrate abundance at solar facilities could also attract insectivorous birds, resulting in a mega-trap by exposing birds to direct impacts associated with the facility; e.g. collision with solar infrastructure or burning due to solar flux (Kagan et al., 2014). Additionally, larger numbers of insectivorous birds could also lead to elevated predation pressure on invertebrates (Horváth et al., 2010; Gibson et al., 2017).

Disturbance and climatic regimes can also change considerably where solar facilities are built. In arid rangelands, grazing livestock are replaced by human foot and vehicle traffic. The structures associated with solar facilities create both rain and sun shadows and also areas with (relatively) higher water run-off. These changes to environmental conditions may also influence invertebrate assemblages, through creation of patches with low and high productivity.

Invertebrates play essential ecological roles in processes that maintain ecosystem integrity including nutrient cycling, pollination, decomposition of organic material and water infiltration (e.g. Losey and Vaugh, 2006), and can be used as indicators of environmental degradation (Whitford, 1996; Seymour and Dean, 1999; Weisser and Siemann, 2008). Therefore, if solar facilities attract invertebrates, they could potentially influence community assemblages in the area with cascading ecological effects.

There are virtually no published studies on the impacts of CSP facilities on invertebrate communities. Diehl et al. (2016) monitored the presence and diversity of insects near CSP towers, but there are no studies on the impacts of CSP parabolic trough facilities. We investigated the impacts on invertebrates of a large CSP trough facility, using two sampling methods to assess epigaeic and flying arthropod communities. We anticipated that certain orders of ground-living invertebrates might increase in response to removal of livestock activities, while others that are usually associated with grazing disturbance and dung might be less abundant in the solar facility. We also hypothesized that CSP parabolic trough facilities will attract flying insects because of the artificial lighting associated with these facilities, and reflection from trough solar collectors. We therefore expected both epigaeic and flying invertebrate assemblages to exhibit differences in relative abundance and composition between facilities and the adjacent rangeland, with greater differences expected for flying invertebrates. We investigated the impacts of a CSP trough facility on invertebrate assemblages by comparing abundance and community composition between the facility and adjacent rangelands. Although this study only addresses differences in invertebrate assemblages at one CSP facility and its surrounds, such an assessment has yet to be reported in the peer-reviewed literature, and we envisage that this work can serve as a model for other studies that will together allow more general conclusions to be drawn.

## 2. Methods

## 2.1. Study site

This study was conducted at the ACWA Power SolAfrica Bokpoort CSP Power Plant (Pty) Ltd (RF), hereafter referred to as “Bokpoort”, one of only two operational CSP trough facilities in South Africa at the time of the study. This 50 Megawatt (MW) parabolic trough CSP facility is located at 28°44.4′ S, 21°59.7′ E in the Northern Cape Province of South Africa, approximately 30 km northwest of Groblershoop (Fig. 1).

Commercial operation of Bokpoort began in March 2016. The facility is situated on the edge of the Nama Karoo and Savannah Biome (Fig. 1), characterised by Kalahari Karroid Shrubland (Mucina and Rutherford, 2006). Dominant species of this vegetation type include small trees (e.g., black thorn Senegalia mellifera), tall shrubs (e.g., three-thorn Rhigozum trichotomum), low shrubs (e.g., steekbossie Hermannia spinosa), and herbaceous species (e.g. karmedik Dicoma capensis and ostrich herb Gisekia africana). The annual precipitation typically is 100–200 mm, and solar radiation recorded here is the highest for the entire Nama Karoo during winter (Mucina and Rutherford, 2006). Land use in the area is predominantly rangeland for livestock and game farming.

The facility has a footprint of ca 250 ha and uses parabolic mirrors to concentrate solar rays onto a receiver tube containing a Heat Transfer Fluid (HTF). The heated HTF is transferred to a power block where it is used to produce steam to drive a turbine. The solar field consists of 360 rows (ca 300 m each) of parabolic mirrors (troughs) giving a total solar collector length of ca 108 km. The rows are divided into 24 sections (consisting of 28 mirrors, each 2.89 × 1.70 m) per row. The facility has two evaporation ponds (200 × 280 m), to dispose of wastewater and two water storage ponds (85 × 85 m). The entire facility is surrounded by a 2.5 m-high single mesh fence.

## 2.2. Invertebrate communities

To assess changes in invertebrate communities, two complementary passive sampling techniques, (pitfall and sticky traps) were deployed in three sampling areas to collect a representative portion of functional groups within the invertebrate community (Coulson et al., 2003). Three sites were sampled (Fig. 1):

1. Power block (PB): Situated in the centre of the facility and is illuminated at night. Traps were deployed within the first three mirror rows surrounding the power block.

2. Solar field (SF): Mirror rows with no artificial lighting; all traps were > 100 m from power block sampling sites).

3. Rangeland (RL): Vegetated habitat outside of the facility currently grazed by livestock. Traps were set up 40–100 m outside the perimeter fence.

Sampling occurred at the start of the austral summer, in three rounds each lasting seven days (starting 10 October, 1 November and 20 November 2016). In each of the three ‘habitats’, five trapping stations were set per sampling round. Each trapping station consisted of one pitfall (for epigaeic invertebrates) and one sticky trap (for flying invertebrates). Traps were set at the same time in all three sampling areas to limit the effects of environmental factors on invertebrate abundance (Coulson et al., 2003). Traps were also set systematically to ensure a representative sample of the study site. Vegetation coverage was taken into account to ensure that sampling was even across different vegetation densities, as well as differing substrates (e.g. gravel and sand). There was a bias towards ease of vehicle access to the sampling points within the solar field. In the rangeland areas, traps were set at least 100 m apart. Pitfall traps consisted of a 500-ml transparent plastic cup (95-mm diameter), filled with ∼120 ml of a 1:1 solution of water and propylene glycol, and buried so that the lip of the cup was flush with the soil surface (Brown and Matthews, 2016). Sticky traps consisted of a pre-glued white cardboard sheet (280 × 200 mm; Delta trap sticky liner, Insect Science (Pty) Ltd), stapled onto thick cardboard and mounted 1.2–1.6 m above the ground, either on an existing structural pole or a wooden stake hammered into the ground. Each sticky trap was set within a 5 m radius of its paired pitfall trap. After one week, samples were removed and stored for later identification in 70% ethanol (Seymour and Dean, 1999) in plastic jars with the date, site and trap number recorded. Sticky traps were covered with plastic film during storage to prevent damaging samples and catching

additional insects outside of the sampling period (Coulson et al., 2003). All invertebrates > 0.5 mm in length were identified to Order using a dissecting microscope, and abundance per trap was recorded.

## 2.3. Statistical analysis

The total number of invertebrates caught per order in each habitat was summed to calculate invertebrate abundance per habitat. Given that pitfall trapping can yield unreliable abundance estimates for social species like ants (Romero and Jaffe, 1989; Mauda et al., 2018), we excluded any traps with abundance of social species of more than two standard deviations above the mean in any calculations involving abundance (i.e., abundance, Shannon diversity and analyses of assemblage composition), in an attempt to exclude skewed abundance estimates arising through traps placed near nests. Order richness, abundance and Shannon diversity Index per trap pair were calculated and assessed for spatial autocorrelation using Moran's I. We assessed differences in order richness, Shannon diversity and abundance per trap for epigaeic (pitfall) and flying (sticky trap) invertebrates using general linear mixed effects models on pitfall and sticky trap catches, respectively. We set order richness, Shannon diversity and abundance per trap as the dependent variables in each model, habitat (i.e., rangeland, solar field or power block) as independent variables, and date of sampling as a random effect, with normal error distribution, but with a Poisson distribution and log-link function for order richness, using the package nlme (Pinheiro et al., 2018) in the R statistical computing environment (R Core Team, 2018). We compared whether random slope or random intercepts were a better fit using Akaike Information Criteria (AIC) and in each case, random intercept models provided a better fit. Violations of model assumptions were assessed using partial residual plots. We also calculated variation explained by fixed and random factors (Nakagawa and Shielzeth, 2013).

To test the null hypothesis of no effect of the solar facility on (i) epigaeic and (ii) flying invertebrate assemblage composition, we fitted generalised linear models to abundances per order for each of the pitfall and sticky traps, respectively, in the R package “mvabund” (Wang et al., 2018) using the “manyglm” and “anova.manyglm” functions. This model-based approach is preferable to distance-based methods, because multivariate generalised linear models can account for confounding mean-variance relationships, which often arise in abundance data containing many zeros (Warton et al., 2012, 2015). The method tests for an effect of habitat by summing likelihood ratio statistics for each order to yield a community-level measure of each habitat. In cases where the number of traps used was not equal (owing to removal of traps that appeared to have been near nests of social species), we included an offset in the model, which we set as the logarithm of the number of traps for each habitat (Warton et al., 2015). We used the PITresidual bootstrap method (Warton et al., 2017) to estimate p values, resampling 999 rows of the dataset. We checked the models for departure from model assumptions by visual assessment of Dunn-Smyth residuals plotted against fitted values. To visualise relative differences in assemblage composition, we plotted the model coefficients for each Order in each habitat, using the “lattice” package (Sarkar, 2008). We also visualised communities using an unconstrained ordination based on latent variable models, run in the “boral” package in R (Hui, 2016, 2018).

## 3.1.1. Epigaeic invertebrates

A total of 7 194 invertebrates were caught during pitfall trapping (Table 1). The power block had the greatest total abundance (3 531) followed by the solar field (2 132) and the rangeland (1 531). Most epigaeic invertebrates were Hymenoptera (76%, n = 5 477) of which 99% were ants (n = 5 412, Table 1). The abundance of ants was nearly twice as high in the power block compared to the solar field and rangeland. However, one trap in the power block appears to have been near to a nest, catching 1 148 ants, well beyond 2 standard deviations of the mean (468). Excluding this trap from the analysis, the number of invertebrates caught at the power block was still fairly high at 2 273, even with one fewer trap (Table 1). After removal of the outlier trap sample, abundance did not differ between habitats (mean = 132.8 ± 80.6, tRL = −1.8, tSF = −0.19; p > 0.05). Ants were still most abundant in the power block, decreasing by approximately 13% in solar field and 26% in rangeland (Table 1). The number of coleopterans and hemipterans was similar between the solar field and power block, but approximately only half as many coleopterans and one twentieth of the hemipterans were trapped in the adjacent rangeland (Table 1).

The rangeland supported more orders (19) than the solar field (13) or power block (12) (Table 1). The mean number of orders per trap (mean ± se = 6.1 ± 0.4) did not differ significantly between habitats (tRL = −0.28, tSF = 1.67, p > 0.05; Fig. 2a), but Shannon diversity was significantly lower in rangeland (mean ± se 0.75 ± 0.11) than the other two habitats (SF and PB 0.96 ± 0.16; tRL = −2.02, p < 0.05; Fig. 2b), although variation in Shannon diversity explained by habitat (8.8%) was much less than that explained by date (38.9%), indicating the importance of date of trapping for this index. An analysis of changes in Shannon diversity with habitat and date as explanatory variables found that this measure was greatest at the first date of sampling (10th October 2018).

## 3.2. Invertebrate assemblage composition

## 3.2.1. Epigaeic invertebrates

There were significant differences in the composition of epigaeic invertebrates between the three habitats (Global test statistic = 128.1, p < 0.001, resid. df = 41, df = 2). The rangeland had significantly different invertebrate assemblages to the power block and solar field, which did not differ from each other (Wald statistics: RL = 9.31, p < 0.001; SF = 3.5, p = 0.24). ## 3.2.2. Flying invertebrates

The composition of flying invertebrate communities differed significantly between all three habitats (global test statistic = 62.68, p < 0.001; residual df = 42, df = 2). However, only two orders showed significant (p < 0.05) differences in abundance between habitats for sticky trapping: Diptera and Hymenoptera. These two orders collectively explained 70% of the observed differences in communities between habitats (Table 2). Diptera had the largest coefficients in the power block, Hymenoptera were most represented in the rangeland (Fig. 4b). Clear separation is not overly evident in the ordination, however for epigaeic invertebrates it appears that the rangeland sites were clustered closer to each other than the other habitats (Fig. 5).

## 4. Discussion

rangelands for either epigaeic or flying invertebrates, assemblage composition differed significantly, even at the very coarse taxonomic level of order. Most differences were between the solar facility and the rangeland, where epigaeic invertebrate assemblages were more diverse. Flying invertebrate communities differed between all three habitats which might be expected, as we anticipated the presence of artificial light at the power block, in addition to the presence of the solar mirrors, to have an effect on invertebrates.

Our findings suggest a combination of factors that could have contributed to changes in invertebrate community composition. Although further research is required to address the extent of the impacts resulting from this change, that the invertebrate assemblages associated with the CSP trough facility in this arid landscape are different from those in the surrounding landscape suggests change to various ecological functions for which invertebrates are key. Invertebrates are often overlooked during environmental impact studies and implementation of environmental management plans at solar energy developments, even though they are crucial to various ecological functions, particularly pollination, nutrient cycling and seed dispersal. In addition to disruption to ecological functions, changes to invertebrate assemblages could have effects that cascade across the food web, influencing invertebrate predators and prey alike, effects that are often not easy to predict (Säterberg et al., 2013). Such changes to food webs fall outside of the scope of this study but certainly warrant further investigation.

This appears to be the first study investigating the effects of a CSP trough facility on invertebrates. Although we found no significant differences in invertebrate abundance between the facility and adjacent

## 4.1. Epigaeic invertebrates

The slightly greater abundance of epigaeic invertebrates in the solar facility might arise because of increased invertebrate activity associated with disturbed areas. Certain species tend to be more abundant in overgrazed degraded areas (Milton and Dean, 1996), and some increase in abundance and/or activity in response to disturbance (e.g. Mauda et al., 2018). Vegetation cover was almost completely absent, except for a few scattered shrubs in the facility, due to intensive vegetation management to reduce fire risk. Invertebrate activity can be greater in areas with reduced vegetation cover (Seymour and Dean, 1999), potentially explaining the greater abundance of invertebrates recorded within traps placed in the facility. The adjacent rangeland hosted the most orders of invertebrates in pitfall traps, but Shannon diversity was significantly lower than in the solar facility. This might be because the mean number of orders per trap did not vary between habitats, but abundance was slightly greater in the solar facility. That there were more orders in the rangeland possibly means that ecological functioning is greater in this less-transformed habitat, as phylogenetic diversity can be a proxy for ecological function (Cadotte et al., 2008).

Invertebrate community composition in epigaeic invertebrates collected in pitfall traps only differed significantly for four orders: Orthoptera, Hemiptera, Diptera and Aranea (spiders). Orthopterans are considered to be important bioindicators as they are sensitive to environmental changes and fill essential positions in foodwebs, both as consumers and a food source (Guido and Gianelle, 2001; Fartmann et al., 2012). Most orthopterans require habitats with high ambient temperatures for optimal growth and development as well as vegetation cover for food and shelter (Guido and Gianelle, 2001; Fartmann et al., 2012). This appears to conflict with our findings of low grasshopper abundance in rangeland relative to the sparsely-vegetated solar facility. Orthoptera may be tolerant of some degree of habitat disturbance, however, given that they may show no response to changes in the fire regime at ordinal level (Andersen and Müller, 2000). Alternatively, they may have been attracted to the solar facility because of both the artificial lighting used at night in the power block and the polarised light produced by the trough collectors.

Diptera and Hemiptera were also both more abundant in the solar facility than in the adjacent rangeland, even in pitfall traps. Attraction to artificial light has been found for a wide variety of arthropods (Longcore et al., 2015), including Hempitera (Pacheco-Tuchuch et al., 2012), Diptera (Bishop et al., 2004), and perhaps Orthoptera (Barghini and De Medeiros, 2012). Similarly, polarised light produced by humanmade objects with smooth surfaces, is known to attract insects (Horváth et al., 2010; Száz et al., 2016). Once in the area, these species may fall into the pitfall traps, explaining their higher abundances.

Spiders were more abundant in rangeland pitfall traps than in the solar facility. Spiders are predators, and predators play essential roles in stabilising food webs and mitigating trophic cascades (Joseph et al., 2017). Other predatory taxa (Mantodea, Solifugae and scorpions) also tended to be more abundant in the rangeland than the solar facility.

Species at higher trophic levels are usually the first to be lost during perturbation events, impacting ecosystem services via cascading ecological effects (Dobson et al., 2006; Joseph et al., 2017). For example, Joseph et al. (2017) found far lower spider abundance in village habitats than in crop fields and rangelands in South Africa. By losing predators, the risk of outbreaks of pests or invasive species increases (Joseph et al., 2017). This is important in the context of solar energy developments as it appears that the construction of the facility reduced the number of predators, which could potentially lead to trophic cascades, impacting the wider community.

## 4.2. Flying invertebrates

The lack of differences in the abundance of flying invertebrates between the three habitats is perhaps surprising, as we had expected

artificial lighting at the power block, and the parabolic reflectors in the solar field, to have a greater effect than vegetation clearing on invertebrate composition. However, there was a trend for more invertebrates at the power block and the greater numbers of flying/highly mobile taxa observed in pitfall traps in the solar facility suggests that aerial insects might well be attracted to the facility.

Differences in invertebrate community composition caught on sticky traps were significant for Diptera and Hymenoptera. Dipterans were most abundant in the power block, followed by the solar field, which may be a consequence of the attractive effect of artificial lighting at night around the power block, and/or reflections from the solar collectors. Dipterans, even non-syrphids, are important pollinators (Orford et al., 2015), and artificial lighting at night may attract them into the solar facility with implications for pollination in the surrounding rangelands. Bees and wasps (Hymenoptera) were more abundant in the rangeland than the solar field or power block, possibly as a result of the lack of vegetation within the facility as bees and wasp species richness and abundance are closely related to plant species richness (Kruess and Tscharntke, 2002). Bees and wasps perform important ecosystem functions, particularly as pollinators, predators and parasitoids. They may be excluded from habitats by nest availability, and so the disturbance and lack of vegetation may partially explain their lower abundance in the solar facility. At the same time, these taxa are attracted to light, so it is possible that if artificial lights were not present at the power block, the abundance of bees and wasps would have been even lower than we recorded.

The concept of ecological traps is still poorly understood (Robertson and Hutto, 2006). For an area to be classified as an ecological trap, a measure of habitat selection (usually abundance) and a measure of habitat quality and impact (e.g. on reproductive success) need to be determined (Battin, 2004). Here, we were only able to measure habitat selection over a short time period, and therefore cannot assess whether the facility is an ecological trap as we have no measure of lasting impact on invertebrates. Future studies could assess invertebrate population dynamics over time to quantify the impact of the solar facility on the invertebrate community. Our study serves as a snapshot in time, however, and allows us to conclude that the facility is affecting invertebrate assemblages. Although the study lasted for only two months, we found changes in invertebrate abundance and community composition. The long-term effects of the installation may be different to what we have found, given that invertebrate phenology fluctuates over time and different patterns or trends might emerge at different times of the year (Seymour and Dean, 1999; Jonas et al., 2002). Date alone did not explain much variation in epigaeic invertebrate abundance, but there was an interaction between treatment and date: in other words, at some times of the year, the effect of treatment is more marked that at other times. Furthermore, much of the variation in Shannon diversity and flying invertebrate abundances were explained by date. This emphasises the importance of longer-term studies, particularly when trying to compare invertebrate population dynamics. In addition to variation within years, as seen in our dataset, there is likely to be variation between years, particularly in arid areas which often experience years that may be far wetter or drier than the mean. These limitations should be borne in mind for environmental impact assessments and management plans.

Our study only sampled over a few months, which could have prevented detection of significant differences between treatments. Nevertheless, a clear signal emerged of such differences. If the study had lasted longer, we may have been able to detect temporal patterns that would allow us to assess the relative influence of the CSP on invertebrates at different times of the year and in wet or dry years. This could possibly inform mitigation strategies e.g. minimising artificial lighting to reduce light pollution and attraction of invertebrates (Department of Environmental Affairs, 2015) at certain times of the year.

Some information is lost by using coarse resolution taxonomic data,

but the use of order-level data still enables effective assessment for among-site assemblage patterns (Driessen and Kirkpatrick, 2017). Finer resolution of data could have revealed even greater differences between the solar facility and adjacent rangelands, but may also have compromised sample size per taxa examined, reducing the power to detect differences.

## 5. Conclusions

This study provides insights into the effect habitat degradation and anthropogenic impacts from the solar energy industry can have on invertebrate communities in an arid environment. While this facility may have a relatively small footprint, the South African Government's target for solar energy of 9.4 GW (9400 MW) by 2030 (Department of Energy, 2016) extrapolates to 13,000–58,000 ha in South Africa alone. Given that solar power is the fastest-growing renewable energy technology in the world (https://www.renewableenergyworld.com/articles/2017/ 10/three-countries-to-account-for-two-thirds-of-global-renewablesgrowth-by-2022.html), there is a need for more research into not only impacts, but trophic cascades and mitigation measures, to reduce the impacts of these facilities on biodiversity.
